title: Existence of Eigenvectors and Triangular Form
---

Over $\RR$, the rotation example shows that an operator need not have any eigenvector. Over an algebraically closed field (Chapter 4), such as $\CC$, this cannot happen.

:::theorem{7.5.1} Existence of eigenvectors
Let $k$ be algebraically closed and let $V \neq \{0\}$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $k$. Then every $\varphi \in \End(V)$ has an eigenvector: there exist $v \in V$, $v \neq 0$, and $\lambda \in k$ with $\varphi(v) = \lambda v$.
:::

:::proof
Let $n = \dim V$ and take any nonzero vector $v \in V$. The $n + 1$ vectors $v$, $\varphi(v), \ldots, \varphi^n(v)$ must be linearly dependent, so there exist $a_0, \ldots, a_n \in k$, not all zero, with $$a_0 v + a_1 \varphi(v) + \cdots + a_n \varphi^n(v) = 0.$$ Let $p(x) = a_0 + a_1 x + \cdots + a_n x^n$, a nonzero polynomial with $p(\varphi)(v) = 0$. It is not a nonzero constant, since $a_0 v \neq 0$ for $a_0 \neq 0$; so $\deg p = d \geq 1$. Since $k$ is algebraically closed, $p$ factors as $p(x) = c(x - \lambda_1) \cdots (x - \lambda_d)$ with $c \neq 0$ and $\lambda_i \in k$ (Proposition [4.3.17](/notes/math-55a/4-3-polynomial-rings-and-field-extensions#proposition-4-3-17)). Because evaluation at $\varphi$ is a ring homomorphism (Proposition [7.2.2](/notes/math-55a/7-2-polynomials-in-an-operator#proposition-7-2-2)), $$p(\varphi) = c(\varphi - \lambda_1) \circ \cdots \circ (\varphi - \lambda_d).$$ This operator is not injective, since it kills $v \neq 0$. A composition of injective maps is injective, so some factor $\varphi - \lambda_i$ is not injective. Hence $\lambda_i$ is an eigenvalue of $\varphi$ (Proposition [7.4.2](/notes/math-55a/7-4-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors#proposition-7-4-2)).
:::

:::note
Equivalently, by Proposition [7.4.8](/notes/math-55a/7-4-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors#proposition-7-4-8)(d), $\chi_\varphi$ has a root because it is a nonconstant polynomial over an algebraically closed field. The proof above avoids determinants. Over $\RR$, it breaks down exactly where $p$ fails to factor into linear factors; we return to real operators in Section [7.10](/notes/math-55a/7-10-real-vector-spaces-and-complexification).
:::

A square matrix $A = (a_{ij})$ is ***upper triangular*** if $a_{ij} = 0$ for $i > j$. If $\mcB = (v_1, \ldots, v_n)$ is a basis of $V$, the matrix $\mcM(\varphi, \mcB)$ is upper triangular if and only if $\varphi(v_j) \in \operatorname{Span}(v_1, \ldots, v_j)$ for every $j$, that is, if and only if each subspace $V_j = \operatorname{Span}(v_1, \ldots, v_j)$ is $\varphi$-invariant.

:::theorem{7.5.2} Upper-triangular form
Let $k$ be algebraically closed, $V$ a finite-dimensional vector space over $k$, and $\varphi \in \End(V)$. Then there is a basis of $V$ in which the matrix of $\varphi$ is upper triangular: $$\mcM(\varphi) = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & & * \\ & \ddots & \\ 0 & & \lambda_n \end{pmatrix}.$$
:::

:::proof
Induction on $n = \dim V$. If $n \leq 1$, every matrix of $\varphi$ is upper triangular.

Let $n \geq 2$ and assume the result in dimension $n - 1$. By Theorem [7.5.1](/notes/math-55a/7-5-existence-of-eigenvectors-and-triangular-form#theorem-7-5-1), $\varphi$ has an eigenvector $v_1$, say $\varphi(v_1) = \lambda_1 v_1$. The line $L = \operatorname{Span}(v_1)$ is $\varphi$-invariant, so $\varphi$ induces $\bar{\varphi} : V/L \to V/L$ with $\bar{\varphi}(q(v)) = q(\varphi(v))$, where $q : V \to V/L$ is the quotient map (Proposition [7.3.5](/notes/math-55a/7-3-invariant-subspaces#proposition-7-3-5)). Intuitively, $\bar{\varphi}$ is “$\varphi$ modulo $v_1$.” Since $\dim(V/L) = n - 1$, the induction hypothesis gives a basis $u_2, \ldots, u_n$ of $V/L$ with $\bar{\varphi}(u_j) \in \operatorname{Span}(u_2, \ldots, u_j)$ for each $j$. Choose $v_j \in V$ with $q(v_j) = u_j$.

The list $(v_1, \ldots, v_n)$ spans $V$: for $v \in V$, write $q(v) = \sum_{j \geq 2} c_j u_j$; then $v - \sum_{j \geq 2} c_j v_j \in \ker(q) = L = \operatorname{Span}(v_1)$. Having $n = \dim V$ elements, it is a basis. Finally, for $j \geq 2$, $$q(\varphi(v_j)) = \bar{\varphi}(u_j) \in \operatorname{Span}(u_2, \ldots, u_j) = q\bigl(\operatorname{Span}(v_2, \ldots, v_j)\bigr),$$ so $\varphi(v_j) \in \operatorname{Span}(v_2, \ldots, v_j) + L = \operatorname{Span}(v_1, \ldots, v_j)$. Together with $\varphi(v_1) = \lambda_1 v_1$, this says the matrix of $\varphi$ in the basis $(v_1, \ldots, v_n)$ is upper triangular. (Its first column is $(\lambda_1, 0, \ldots, 0)^t$, and its lower right $(n-1) \times (n-1)$ block is the matrix of $\bar{\varphi}$ in the basis $(u_2, \ldots, u_n)$, as in Proposition [7.3.5](/notes/math-55a/7-3-invariant-subspaces#proposition-7-3-5).)
:::

The diagonal of a triangular matrix carries the information about invertibility and eigenvalues. The next two results hold over any field.

:::lemma{7.5.3} Invertibility from the diagonal
Let $\varphi \in \End(V)$ have an upper-triangular matrix $A = (a_{ij})$ in the basis $(v_1, \ldots, v_n)$. Then $\varphi$ is invertible if and only if all the diagonal entries $a_{11}, \ldots, a_{nn}$ are nonzero.
:::

:::proof
Write $V_j = \operatorname{Span}(v_1, \ldots, v_j)$, with $V_0 = \{0\}$.

Suppose all $a_{jj} \neq 0$. We show by induction on $j$ that $v_j \in \Img(\varphi)$. Since $\varphi(v_j) = a_{jj} v_j + \sum_{i < j} a_{ij} v_i$, $$v_j = \frac{1}{a_{jj}}\Bigl(\varphi(v_j) - \sum_{i < j} a_{ij} v_i\Bigr),$$ and the right side lies in $\Img(\varphi)$ because $v_1, \ldots, v_{j-1}$ do. So $\Img(\varphi)$ contains a basis, $\varphi$ is surjective, and hence invertible (Corollary [6.1.16](/notes/math-55a/6-1-kernel-and-image#corollary-6-1-16)).

Suppose $a_{jj} = 0$ for some $j$. Then $\varphi(v_j) \in V_{j-1}$, and also $\varphi(V_{j-1}) \subseteq V_{j-1}$, so $\varphi$ maps the $j$-dimensional space $V_j$ into the $(j-1)$-dimensional space $V_{j-1}$. By Corollary [6.1.15](/notes/math-55a/6-1-kernel-and-image#corollary-6-1-15), $\varphi|_{V_j}$ is not injective, so $\varphi$ is not injective and not invertible.
:::

:::corollary{7.5.4} Eigenvalues from a triangular matrix
Let $\varphi \in \End(V)$ have an upper-triangular matrix $A = (a_{ij})$ in some basis. Then:

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. $\lambda \in k$ is an eigenvalue of $\varphi$ $\iff$ $\varphi - \lambda$ is not invertible $\iff$ $\lambda = a_{jj}$ for some $j$.
2. $\chi_\varphi(x) = (x - a_{11})(x - a_{22}) \cdots (x - a_{nn})$, and the number of times an eigenvalue $\lambda$ appears on the diagonal of $A$ is its algebraic multiplicity.

In particular, every upper-triangular matrix representing $\varphi$ has the same diagonal entries, up to order.
:::

:::proof
(a) The first equivalence is Proposition [7.4.2](/notes/math-55a/7-4-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors#proposition-7-4-2). For the second, apply Lemma [7.5.3](/notes/math-55a/7-5-existence-of-eigenvectors-and-triangular-form#lemma-7-5-3) to $\varphi - \lambda$, whose matrix $A - \lambda I$ is upper triangular with diagonal entries $a_{jj} - \lambda$.

(b) The matrix $xI - A$ is upper triangular with diagonal entries $x - a_{jj}$, and the determinant of a triangular matrix, over $k[x]$ as over $k$, is the product of its diagonal entries (Proposition [5.4.10](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants#proposition-5-4-10)). The statement about multiplicities is Lemma [7.4.11](/notes/math-55a/7-4-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors#lemma-7-4-11). The last sentence follows because $\chi_\varphi$ does not depend on the basis.
:::

:::note
Together, Theorem [7.5.2](/notes/math-55a/7-5-existence-of-eigenvectors-and-triangular-form#theorem-7-5-2) and Corollary [7.5.4](/notes/math-55a/7-5-existence-of-eigenvectors-and-triangular-form#corollary-7-5-4) show that over an algebraically closed field $\chi_\varphi$ splits into linear factors, its roots being the diagonal entries of any triangular matrix of $\varphi$. We will soon see a more conceptual description of the algebraic multiplicity: it is the dimension of the generalized eigenspace (Theorem [7.6.14](/notes/math-55a/7-6-generalized-eigenspaces#theorem-7-6-14)).
:::
